source_metadata.title: Effectiveness of Oseltamivir in Hospitalized Children With Laboratory-Confirmed Influenza, 2014-2023
source_metadata.source_type: journal article; original investigation; retrospective cohort study
source_metadata.supplements: Supplement 1 and Supplement 2 are referenced in the article but are not embedded in the retrieved PDF.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether oseltamivir treatment was associated with lower risk of ICU admission and shorter hospital length of stay among children hospitalized with influenza.
The investigators conducted a retrospective cohort study using FluSurv-NET, a population-based surveillance network covering laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations across 13 US states.
Eligible participants were children younger than 18 years hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza who had a recorded respiratory symptom onset date.

population.label: Children <18 years hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza

atoms.canonical_statement: Exclusions included missing key dates, influenza testing outside the prespecified admission window, hospital transfers, observation encounters, length of stay of 1 day or less or more than 30 days, implausible treatment timing, and use of antivirals other than oseltamivir; same-day oseltamivir initiation and ICU admission was additionally excluded from the primary ICU analysis.

population.label: FluSurv-NET pediatric influenza hospitalization cohort
exclusion_criteria: Missing positive influenza test, oseltamivir initiation, or symptom start dates
Positive influenza test >7 days before or >3 days after admission
Treatment >14 days before admission or prior to symptom onset
Same-day oseltamivir initiation and ICU admission for primary ICU analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The analysis included influenza seasons 2014-2015 through 2022-2023, excluding 2020-2021 because of low influenza hospitalization counts during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Oseltamivir receipt was modeled as a time-dependent exposure anchored at respiratory symptom onset, accounting for exposed and unexposed person-time.

exposures.details: Time-dependent exposure anchored at respiratory symptom onset

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary comparator was no oseltamivir treatment during the relevant risk period.
The primary outcome was ICU admission, modeled as time from respiratory symptom onset to ICU admission.

outcome.definition: Time from respiratory symptom onset to ICU admission

atoms.canonical_statement: The secondary outcome was hospital length of stay, modeled as time from hospital admission to discharge.

outcome.definition: Time from hospital admission to discharge

atoms.canonical_statement: Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with oseltamivir as a time-dependent exposure were used to mitigate immortal time bias.

A priori covariates included age, influenza vaccination status, predominant influenza A subtype, and race and ethnicity; days of illness before hospitalization and ICU admission were additional a priori covariates in the length-of-stay model.
Patients without ICU admission were censored at discharge, and in-hospital deaths were treated as censoring events because death was infrequent.

The investigators tested the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residual correlations and plots, assessed multicollinearity with Spearman correlations, used two-sided tests with P<.05, and performed analyses in SAS 9.4.
Mean hospital length of stay was derived from model-based survival curves with covariates fixed at reference values, and 95% confidence intervals were estimated by bootstrap resampling.
Sensitivity analyses varied classification of same-day treatment and outcome, excluded prehospital oseltamivir, and reincorporated hospitalizations with length of stay of 1 day or less.
Treatment timing was categorized as early oseltamivir (2 days or less from respiratory symptom onset), late oseltamivir (3 days or more from symptom onset), or no oseltamivir.

atoms.canonical_statement: Across 8 seasons, 13,127 hospitalized children with laboratory-confirmed influenza were reported in the FluSurv-NET catchment area; 10,066 (76.7%) received oseltamivir before study exclusions.

population.label: All reported pediatric FluSurv-NET influenza hospitalizations before analytic exclusions

atoms.canonical_statement: The hospital length-of-stay analysis included 7,103 children, of whom 5,746 (80.9%) received oseltamivir.
The ICU admission analysis included 6,044 children, of whom 4,240 (70.2%) received oseltamivir before ICU admission.
In the 7,103-child length-of-stay cohort, median age was 3 years (IQR, 1-7 years).
In Table 1, 3,982 of 7,103 children (56%) were male and 3,121 (44%) were female.
In the length-of-stay cohort, 3,563 children (50%) had at least one medical comorbidity and 1,914 (27%) had asthma.
Oseltamivir was initiated before hospital admission in 1,609 children (22.7%) in the length-of-stay cohort.

exposures.details: Time-dependent exposure anchored at respiratory symptom onset

atoms.canonical_statement: Compared with untreated children, oseltamivir recipients were more often hospitalized within 2 days of symptom onset (49% vs 28%), were age 2 years or younger (45% vs 40%), had medical comorbidity (52% vs 42%), and had asthma (28% vs 23%).
Before adjustment, ICU admission was more common among oseltamivir recipients than nonrecipients (31% vs 15%), and mechanical ventilation was also more common (6% vs 3%).
Time-dependent oseltamivir treatment was associated with a lower adjusted hazard of ICU admission than no treatment (aHR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60-0.80).

atoms.canonical_statement: When children starting oseltamivir on the same day as ICU admission were included and classified as untreated, the adjusted hazard ratio for ICU admission was 0.30 (95% CI, 0.26-0.34).

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that oseltamivir treatment in children hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza was associated with lower likelihood of ICU admission and shorter hospital length of stay and supported treatment as soon as possible regardless of time from symptom onset or underlying risk factors.
The study was retrospective and combined data across multiple sites and seasons, creating inherent variation despite standardized abstraction and adjustment for surveillance site.
Influenza testing was performed at clinician or facility discretion, so children with influenza-like illness without laboratory confirmation were not represented.
FluSurv-NET data came from 13 states covering approximately 9% of the US population, limiting nationwide generalizability.
Time was measured in whole days, and respiratory symptom onset date could be misclassified when fever preceded respiratory symptoms.
Oseltamivir received before hospitalization may have been incompletely captured, creating possible exposure misclassification.
The analysis did not account for the complex survey design used to select cases for case-report-form completion in the 2022-2023 season.
Because the study was observational, the investigators could not account for all potential confounders.

The study was supported by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention through an Emerging Infections Program cooperative agreement and a Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists cooperative agreement.

The funding organization was involved in study design and conduct, data collection and management, analysis and interpretation, manuscript preparation/review/approval, and the decision to submit for publication.

Several authors reported grants or cooperative-agreement support from the CDC or other organizations, and some reported outside consulting, editorial, or industry relationships; the article states that no other disclosures were reported.
The article directs readers to Supplement 2 for the data sharing statement.

extraction_limitations: The retrieved PDF is the 10-page main article only. Supplement 1 (eFigures/eTables containing additional sensitivity and subgroup details) and Supplement 2 (data sharing statement) are referenced but were not embedded in the retrieved PDF; only supplement-derived values repeated in the main article were atomized.

The abstract contains internally inconsistent sex counts/percentages (3382 [56%] male and 3721 [44%] female) relative to the stated 6044-person ICU cohort and Table 1. Baseline sex atoms therefore use Table 1 values for the 7103-person LOS cohort (3982 male, 3121 female) rather than reconciling the abstract by inference.
Atoms marked needs_review have passed structural and sufficiency checks but have not been independently human-verified.
No external sources were used to verify guideline currency, causal interpretation, or supplemental data.
